newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK fears of "censorship" over China dissident book.
newsitem.headline: HK fears of "censorship" over China dissident book.

text.p: Human rights groups in Hong Kong expressed concern on Monday about apparent self-censorship here by distributors of a book by China's best-known dissident Wei Jingsheng, now in jail.

Fears grew after the South China Morning Post newspaper reported that Wei's writings may have been labelled by the Penguin publishing group as too sensitive to promote the anthology of essays and letters in Hong Kong. Representatives of the firm were not immediately available to comment.

China will recover the British-ruled territory in just five weeks from now, and Chinese dissidents living in exile here, along with local pro-democracy activists, have predicted repressive rule after the change of flag.
The looming handover has generated immense sensitivity.

Increasing signs of self-censorship have been evident in the Hong Kong media in recent months and in companies which rely heavily on China business, wary about riling Beijing with gloomy predictions about the handover or negative comments on China.
Wei's book, "The Courage to Stand Alone", has just been published under Penguin's Viking label and the Post devoted a full page last Saturday to extracts.
"We are not trying to sell it actively," the Post on Monday quoted Katherine Lee, sales and marketing executive for Penguin in Hong Kong, as saying.

"For this one I'm not doing anything. It's very sensitive -- especially during the handover period," she was quoted as saying. Lee could not be contacted by Reuters on Monday for further details, and a colleague said Lee had gone on leave.
Penguin's regional sales and marketing manager Claire Cumming was out of town and could not be reached for comment.
"If it's true it's very disturbing, because books like this have always been sold in Hong Kong," said John Schidlovsky, who heads the local office of the New York-based Freedom Forum.
"It would be a disturbing sign of self-censorship. It's not necessary to take steps like this," he told Reuters.
"The Chinese government has made no secret of the fact it despises Weij Jingsheng, and it's clear they wouldn't want this book distributed in China," he added.
A publishing source told Reuters the only outlet he was aware of selling the book in Hong Kong so far was the chain of South China Morning Post Family Bookshops.

At the Hong Kong office of the London-based human rights group Amnesty International, China researcher Catherine Baber was also disturbed by the possibility that the book had become a victim of self-censorship.
"We're operating on the basis that it's business as usual in Hong Kong. It's entirely regrettable (if this has happened). It's self-censorship in yet another area," Baber told Reuters.
"Especially when other books about Wei and other dissidents are freely on sale here," she added.
The 47-year-old Wei is China's best-known dissident and regarded as the father of China's democracy movement.

He was jailed in 1979 for counter-revolutionary incitement after advocating democratic change, referring to democracy as China's much-needed "fifth modernisation", and spent 14 and a half years in prison. In 1994 after his release he was detained again and was later sentenced for a further 14 years.
Chinese dissidents abroad arranged publication of Wei's writings in the book, which include strong denunciations of China's leader Deng Xiaoping, who died in February this year.
Wei has a strong following in Hong Kong, and local activists regularly gather thousands of signatures on petitions calling for his release.
